prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators and its first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: The Kane-Mele Z2 classification and the Molenkamp HgTe observation of edge transport form a rare, clean case in which a general conceptual principle was predicted and then confirmed quantitatively in a specific material within about two years. Fifteen to twenty years of independent confirmation, from transport to photoemission in many compounds, has left the interpretation stable. Topology in band structure has reshaped how condensed matter is classified and has fed into superconductivity and quantum-computing proposals. Of the candidates, this one combines discovery-level originality with the broadest independent confirmation, and it is the only configuration among my top choices where theory and experiment are tightly linked and timing is neither early nor late.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with the 2016 prize for topological phase transitions and phases of matter, which a committee could regard as already having honoured the topological idea. Attribution is also genuinely hard. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed HgTe as the platform and are not among the credited names, Hasan's three-dimensional work is excluded from my trio, and Fu, Kane and Mele versus Moore and Balents is a known sticking point. A three-person prize cannot fairly cover the full two- and three-dimensional story.

responses.point: Olsson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first as a concrete before-and-after discovery with a theory-plus-experiment pairing, but notes that the topological-insulator case must rest on what is new relative to 2016.
responses.response: I accept her 2016 caveat and consider it the main obstacle to B008. But the 2016 prize honoured topological phase transitions and the quantum Hall-type phases; it did not recognise time-reversal-invariant topological insulators or the quantum spin Hall edge states, which are a distinct principle with a separate experimental confirmation. On twisted bilayer graphene I disagree about timing. The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unresolved and the discovery is only eight years old, so I would rather wait than reward it now. I keep it as an alternative and am open to moving it up if colleagues argue the flat-band and correlated-insulator discovery is mature on its own.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the IceCube neutrino discovery first and puts topological insulators second with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, crediting Hasan for the first three-dimensional topological insulators by photoemission.
responses.response: I agree with him that topological insulators deserve a high place, but disagree about Hasan. I would anchor the prize in the quantum spin Hall effect, where theory and experiment are paired (Kane and Mele, then Molenkamp), and not mix 2D and 3D results, since Fu-Kane-Mele and Moore-Balents priority in 3D is contested and could not be settled with Hasan alone. Leaving out Mele, as his trio does, is a worse omission to me, because the Z2 classification is the central idea. On IceCube I am persuaded that the discovery is real, but a collaboration of hundreds makes a three-name attribution arbitrary, and the source identification is still at moderate significance.

responses.point: Lindroth puts optical lattice clocks first as a clean, original and consequential advance in metrology, with a coherent two-name configuration, and ranks topological insulators low, outside her field.
responses.response: The clock case is strong on maturity and attribution, and the two-person configuration is the cleanest on the shortlist; I keep it as a serious alternative, higher than I ranked it in my opening ballot. My reservation is conceptual. It is a superb refinement of the frequency-standard programme that already earned the 2005 and 2012 prizes, whereas the Z2 classification introduced a principle that did not exist before. I would not call the clock merely technical, but I would ask what physics a clock prize teaches that those earlier prizes did not.

responses.point: Kroll weighs most heavily advances in what we can measure and how accurately, and gives the lattice clock first place for its 1e-18 uncertainty and its use in tests of constants and relativistic geodesy.
responses.response: I take the force of that criterion, and the clock case does rest on instrument-level consequences that are verified, not promised. I would ask whether the physics gain so far is the clock itself or tests it makes possible, since no deviation from existing theory has yet been seen, and a redefinition of the second is still pending. I do not think that makes the prize premature. It is why I prefer to put a concept with wide downstream influence first and the clock close behind.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the 2016 topological prize as overlapping enough to disqualify or discount B008.
Whether the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal should displace Mele or sit alongside Kane and Molenkamp, which the credited names do not allow.
Whether the pairing mechanism for magic-angle graphene will be settled enough in the next few years to change my view of its maturity.

My own opening ballot ranked fluctuation theorems first, but only I supported it and credit is diffuse among Jarzynski, Crooks, Evans, Seifert, Gallavotti, Cohen and Kurchan; I have not verified the priority dates and have lowered it as a prize candidate.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile; none of the credited names for B008, B029 or B043 appears among the documented connections, and my own area (stochastic processes, turbulence, neural networks) does not overlap with these candidates.
